title: APIs & Web Services
description: How systems talk over HTTP: REST, status codes, authentication, documentation and real-time options.
resumo: REST: resources in URLs, HTTP verbs, no session state on the server.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not — payments use an Idempotency-Key. GET never changes data.
Status: 200, 201, 204 | 400, 401 (not authenticated), 403 (not allowed), 404, 409 | 500, 503. Never 200 with an error inside.
Errors in one standard format: Problem Details (RFC 9457).
Lists are always paginated (page, size, sort), with a cap on the size; cursor pagination for huge lists.
JWT is the token format; OAuth 2.0 is how you get it; OIDC adds login. The JWT payload is readable by anyone.
CORS is a browser rule — Postman ignores it. Allow only known origins.
Document with OpenAPI; springdoc generates the spec from your controllers.

subsections.subtitle: What Is an API?
subsections.description: A contract between systems, usually spoken over HTTP.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the web frontend, the mobile app and a partner system all need the same data. Giving each of them direct access to the database exposes everything and ties them all to its tables.

**Concept:** an API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract: the operations a system offers, with their inputs and outputs, hiding how they are implemented. Web APIs use HTTP: the client sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body) and the server returns a response (status code, headers, body), usually JSON.

**How it works:** the API can change its internals — database, language, servers — as long as the contract stays the same. Clients only depend on the contract.
examples.code:
$ curl -i https://api.example.com/users/1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":1,"name":"Ana"}

$ curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"name":"Bruno"}'
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /users/2
examples.interview_question: What is an API, and what does an HTTP request and response contain?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Sending JSON without the `Content-Type` header. `curl -d` sends the body as a form by default, and Spring answers 415 Unsupported Media Type, because it does not know the body is JSON.
examples.code:
# WRONG: no Content-Type -> 415 Unsupported Media Type
curl -X POST localhost:8080/users -d '{"name":"Bruno"}'

# RIGHT
curl -X POST localhost:8080/users -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Bruno"}'

subsections.subtitle: REST
subsections.description: Resources in URLs, actions in HTTP methods.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** without conventions, every API invents its own style — `/getUser`, `/doCreateUser`, `/deleteUserNow` — and every client has to learn each one.

**Concept:** REST is an architectural style. Resources are identified by URLs, written as nouns (`/orders/42`); the HTTP method says what to do (GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH change some fields, DELETE remove); and data travels as representations, usually JSON. REST is stateless: each request carries everything needed, such as the token, so any server instance can answer it.

**How it works:** statelessness is what lets you add more instances behind a load balancer. Related resources nest in the URL (`/customers/7/orders`). Hypermedia links in responses (HATEOAS) are the most complete level of REST, but rarely used in practice.
examples.code:
GET    /orders                list orders
GET    /orders/42             one order
POST   /orders                create one       -> 201 Created + Location: /orders/43
PUT    /orders/42             replace order 42
PATCH  /orders/42             change some fields
DELETE /orders/42             remove it        -> 204 No Content
GET    /customers/7/orders    the orders of customer 7
examples.interview_question: What are the principles of REST, and how does statelessness help scalability?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Verbs in the URL and POST for everything. The method no longer says what happens, so caches, retries and tools cannot rely on it. For an action that is not plain CRUD, a sub-resource such as `POST /orders/42/cancellation` is fine.
examples.code:
# WRONG: actions in the URL, everything is POST
POST /getOrder?id=42
POST /deleteOrder?id=42

# RIGHT: the resource in the URL, the action in the method
GET    /orders/42
DELETE /orders/42

subsections.subtitle: HTTP Status Codes
subsections.description: Telling the client what happened, in three digits.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** if every response is 200 with `{"error": ...}` in the body, clients, monitoring and caches cannot tell success from failure.

**Concept:** the first digit gives the class: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error (the request must change), 5xx server error (the server failed; retrying later may work). The most used: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content; 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Content; 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable.

**How it works:** pick the most specific code. 401 means "who are you?" and 403 "I know who you are, and the answer is no". 409 fits a conflict with the current state, such as a duplicate email. A 500 should never be returned on purpose.
examples.code:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /users/43

// Spring
return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/users/" + id)).body(user);    // 201
return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();                              // 204
throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Email already registered");   // 409
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between 401 and 403? Name other 2xx, 4xx and 5xx codes and when to use them.

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Returning 200 with an error in the body. HTTP says it worked, so monitoring counts it as success and clients must parse the body to find out.

subsections.subtitle: Authentication and Authorization
subsections.description: Who is calling, and what they are allowed to do.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the API has to know who is calling, to show "my orders", and whether that caller may do what they ask — only admins delete products.

**Concept:** authentication answers "who are you?" (login, token). Authorization answers "what may you do?" (roles, scopes, ownership). APIs usually receive a bearer token in the `Authorization` header. JWT is a token format: header.payload.signature, Base64url-encoded — readable, not encrypted — and signed, so the API can check it without a database lookup. OAuth 2.0 is the framework that defines how a client obtains an access token (often a JWT). OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds identity on top of OAuth 2.0 — "log in with Google".

**How it works:** a missing or invalid token gets 401; a valid token without permission gets 403. Tokens always travel over HTTPS.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and how do JWT, OAuth 2.0 and OIDC fit together?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Putting sensitive data in the JWT payload, assuming it is encrypted. It is only encoded: anyone with the token can decode it. Keep identifiers and permissions in the token, and look up the rest on the server.

subsections.subtitle: API Documentation
subsections.description: OpenAPI and Swagger UI, generated from the code.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the frontend team asks every week which fields an endpoint returns, and an outdated wiki page sends them the wrong ones.

**Concept:** OpenAPI (formerly the Swagger specification) describes an HTTP API in YAML or JSON: paths, parameters, request and response bodies, authentication. Swagger UI renders it as an interactive page where you can try the calls. The spec can be generated from the code (code-first) or written first and used to generate code (contract-first).

**How it works:** with the springdoc dependency, Spring Boot generates the spec from your controllers and DTOs — validation annotations included. `@Operation` and `@ApiResponse` add descriptions where the code alone is not enough.
examples.code:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
  <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
  <version>2.6.0</version>   <!-- springdoc 2.x for Spring Boot 3 -->
</dependency>

@Operation(summary = "Find a user by id")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "User not found")
@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
public UserResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

// Swagger UI: http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html    Spec: /v3/api-docs
examples.interview_question: Why document APIs, and how does OpenAPI/Swagger help?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Leaving Swagger UI open in production for an internal API. It hands anyone a complete map of the endpoints, ready to try. Disable or protect it there, and keep it in development and test.
examples.code:
# application-prod.yml
springdoc:
  api-docs:
    enabled: false
  swagger-ui:
    enabled: false

subsections.subtitle: HTTP Methods and Idempotency
subsections.description: Which requests are safe to repeat.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a payment request times out. Did it go through? The client retries — and the customer may be charged twice.

**Concept:** a safe method does not change state (GET, HEAD). An idempotent method has the same effect whether it runs once or many times: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, because each call can create something new; PATCH depends on how it is implemented.

**How it works:** clients and proxies can retry idempotent requests safely. For a POST that must never run twice, such as a payment, the client sends an `Idempotency-Key` header; the server stores the key with the first result and returns that result again for a repeated key.
examples.code:
GET    /orders/42        -> reads (safe and idempotent)
PUT    /orders/42        -> replaces the whole resource (idempotent)
PATCH  /orders/42        -> changes some fields
DELETE /orders/42        -> removes (idempotent: the 2nd call returns 404 or 204)
POST   /orders           -> creates (NOT idempotent)

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c2a10-9b1e-4c55-a2d1-55e0c1f9a001
examples.interview_question: Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and why does it matter?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A GET that changes data. Browsers prefetch links, crawlers follow them and proxies retry GETs, so the action runs without anyone asking for it.
examples.code:
# WRONG: a GET that cancels
GET /orders/42/cancel

# RIGHT
POST /orders/42/cancellation

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an unbounded `GET /orders` is slow, and as the table grows it can take the application down with an `OutOfMemoryError`.

**Concept:** return collections in pages, with `page`, `size` and `sort` parameters; Spring Data turns them into a `Pageable` automatically. Offset pagination (`OFFSET 10000`) gets slower on high pages; for very large or fast-changing lists, cursor (keyset) pagination — "items after id X" — stays fast.

**How it works:** an optional filter that is null cannot go straight into `findByCategory`: Spring Data would generate `category IS NULL` and return almost nothing. Branch on the filter, or use a Specification.
examples.interview_question: How do you implement pagination in a REST API with Spring?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Letting the client choose any page size. `size=1000000` turns pagination off. Cap it.
examples.code:
# WRONG: the client controls the size without limit
GET /products?size=1000000

# RIGHT: cap the page size (Spring Data's default cap is 2000)
spring:
  data:
    web:
      pageable:
        max-page-size: 100

subsections.subtitle: Standard Errors (Problem Details)
subsections.description: One error format for the whole API, RFC 9457.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** each endpoint returns errors in its own shape — `{"msg"}`, `{"error"}`, plain text — so clients need special code for each one.

**Concept:** RFC 9457 (Problem Details, the successor of RFC 7807) defines a standard JSON error body with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`, plus extra fields of your own, served as `application/problem+json`. Spring supports it natively with `ProblemDetail`, and `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` applies it to Spring's own errors too.

**How it works:** return a `ProblemDetail` from your `@RestControllerAdvice` handlers. Clients handle every error the same way.
examples.interview_question: How do you standardize the body of an API's error responses?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Putting the raw message of an unexpected exception in `detail`. It can contain SQL, table names or internal paths — useful to an attacker. For unexpected errors, return a generic message with an id, and keep the details in the log.

subsections.subtitle: CORS
subsections.description: Why the browser blocks calls between origins.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the frontend at `https://app.example.com` calls the API at `https://api.example.com`. It works in Postman, but the browser blocks it.

**Concept:** CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser rule: a page may only read responses from another origin if that server allows it with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. For methods or headers that are not "simple", the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` preflight request. Postman, curl and server-to-server calls do not apply CORS — which also means CORS is not protection for your API; authentication is.

**How it works:** configure the allowed origins, methods and headers on the API. Allow only the origins you know.
examples.interview_question: What is CORS, and why does a call work in Postman but fail in the browser?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Allowing every origin (`*`) together with credentials. Spring rejects this combination, and it would let any website make authenticated calls with your users' cookies. List the known origins.
